entry: Visual art made in the context of folk culture, generally by makers trained within a popular rather than fine-art tradition. Its objects usually have practical utility rather than being exclusively decorative, and they are usually one-offs rather than mass-produced. The concept originated in Europe and is distinctly 19th-century. Critic Edward Lucie-Smith described folk art as "unsophisticated art, both fine and applied, which is supposedly rooted in the collective awareness of simple people." Alois Riegl's 1894 study stressed that individual makers still shape traditions within inherited forms. Quilting, decoy carving and ornamental picture framing continue to be practiced. Folk art overlaps with naive art and includes [[Ceramic|ceramics]], textiles and weather vanes, and [[Outsider art|outsider art]] is a subtype.

Dance that reflects the life of the people of a certain country or region. Folk dances are typically performed at social gatherings or community events by people with little or no professional training, often to traditional or folk music. They usually originate as participatory activities rather than staged performances, and new dancers learn them informally by observing and imitating. Dances of [[Ritual|ritual]] origin are generally not considered folk dances. Modern street styles such as [[Hip-hop]] are usually called vernacular dances instead. Balfolk events, popular mainly in Western and Central Europe, feature regional dances from France, Sweden and Spain alongside 19th-century partner dances such as the polka and [[Waltz]].

Forms of religion distinct from the doctrines and practices of organized religion, also called traditional, vernacular or popular religion. It consists of ethnic or regional customs within a major faith but outside its formal doctrine. Scholars use the term for two related subjects: the religious dimension of [[Folklore|folk culture]], and the syncretism that results when formal religion mixes with folk cultures, as with Vodun and Santería, which blended African beliefs with Roman Catholicism. [[Chinese folk religion]], folk [[Hinduism]], folk [[Christianity]] and folk [[Islam]] are examples. In China, folk Protestantism originated with the [[Taiping Rebellion]]. Clergy also use the term for people who rarely attend worship but want religious weddings or funerals or, among Christians, baptism for their children.

American rock band formed in [[Seattle]] in 1994. Initially a one-man project of former [[Nirvana (band)|Nirvana]] drummer Dave Grohl, the band has won 15 [[Grammy Awards]], including Best Rock Album five times. It was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2021, its first year of eligibility.

Classification of foods grouped by similar nutritional properties or biological origin, used in nutrition guides. Food groups were devised in public health education to teach people with very restricted, unvaried diets how to avoid nutritional deficiencies, and were later adapted to diet-related diseases such as obesity, diabetes and heart disease. Classical Greek opson and sitos were used for moral education, and the concept of mitahara appears in early-first-millennium [[Sanskrit]] texts. In the United States the USDA promoted eight basic food groups before 1943, then seven until 1956 and then four. Common categories include dairy, [[Fruit|fruits]], cereals, [[Legume|legumes]] and [[Meat|meat]]. Researchers criticized food groups from the 1980s, arguing that nutritional deficiencies were no longer major causes of diet-related disease in affluent societies.

Collective term for diverse businesses that supply most of the world's food. The industry includes [[Agriculture|agriculture]], manufacture of agrichemicals and farm machinery, food processing, [[Marketing|marketing]], wholesale distribution, food service, [[Retail|retailing]], regulation, education, research and development, and financial services. Manufacturing ranges from small, labor-intensive family operations to large, capital-intensive, highly mechanized plants. On average, 83% of the food humans consume is produced by terrestrial agriculture, with aquaculture and [[Fishing|fishing]] also playing vital roles. Only subsistence farmers and [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherers]] lie outside the modern food industry. Its dominant companies are sometimes called Big Food, a term coined by the writer Neil Hamilton.

Illness caused by eating food contaminated with [[Pathogen|pathogens]], prions or toxins. Also called food poisoning, it can come from [[Bacteria|bacteria]] such as [[Salmonella]], [[Norovirus|viruses]] such as norovirus, parasites, [[Prion|prions]] (the agents of mad cow disease), and toxins such as aflatoxins in peanuts. Symptoms often include vomiting, fever, aches, and diarrhea and dehydration, and many effects result from the body's immune response. Symptoms may appear within hours or days, depending on the cause and the quantity eaten. In low- and middle-income countries in 2010, foodborne disease caused an estimated 600 million illnesses and 420,000 deaths, with an economic loss estimated at US$110 billion annually. Public health experts consider regular hand-washing one of the most effective defenses against it.

Terminal part of the limb of many [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]], which bears weight and allows locomotion. In many animals it is an organ made up of one or more segments or [[Bone|bones]], generally including claws or nails. The human foot contains 26 bones, 33 [[Joint|joints]] (20 of them actively articulated), and more than 100 [[Muscle|muscles]], [[Tendon|tendons]] and [[Ligament|ligaments]]. It is divided into the hindfoot, midfoot and forefoot. The talus and calcaneus of the hindfoot connect to the tibia and [[Fibula|fibula]] to form the ankle. The five irregular midfoot bones form arches that act as shock absorbers, and the forefoot has five toes. An anthropometric study of 1,197 North American adult men found a foot length of 26.3 cm with a standard deviation of 1.2 cm. The word foot comes from [[Old English]] fot.

Former Chinese custom of breaking and tightly binding girls' feet to alter their shape and size. Bound feet, called lotus feet, were a status symbol and mark of feminine beauty in late imperial China. The practice spread from elite circles of the [[Song dynasty]] to lower social classes by the [[Qing dynasty]], causing lifelong disabilities. By the 19th century an estimated 40–50% of Chinese women may have had bound feet. Reformers and Christian missionaries challenged it in the late 19th century, and it died out in the early 20th century.

Sexual interest in [[Foot|feet]], also known as podophilia. Attraction ranges from admiring feet to sexual activity in which feet are the only way to climax. In 2006 it was the most commonly discussed type of partialist fantasy in pornographic Internet forums, and studies estimate that 14% of Americans have involved feet in sex at least once in their lifetime. Contemporary psychiatric institutions regard it as a valid expression of [[Human sexuality|human sexuality]] unless it involves non-consensual contact, theft of footwear or considerable distress.

Unit of length in the British [[Imperial units|imperial]] and United States customary systems. One foot comprises [[Inch|12 inches]], and since an international agreement in 1959 it has been exactly 0.3048 meters. Historically the foot varied from about 250 mm to 335 mm across the Greek, Roman, Chinese, French and English systems. The Roman foot was divided into 12 unciae, the source of the English words inch and ounce. In 790 [[Charlemagne]] tried to reform measures based on a toise of six feet, without establishing a single standard. The United States uses the foot in preference to the [[Metric system|meter]] in many commercial and engineering activities, and it is legally recognized in the United Kingdom and as an alternative in Canada. International [[Aviation|aviation]] uses it for altitude, as the flight level unit.

Family of team sports in which players move a ball into a goal or over a goal line using only the body. Forms include [[Association football]], [[American football]], [[Australian rules football]], [[Rugby league]] and [[Rugby union]], which share common origins. Codified versions emerged at English public schools in the 19th century, and the [[British Empire]] spread the rules. Professionalism was allowed in English association football in 1885, and the Football League followed three years later.

Phylum of single-celled amoeboid [[Protist|protists]] in the [[Rhizaria]] group, most of them marine. Their name is Latin for hole bearers, after the openings between the chambers of their shells. Most species live on or in seafloor [[Sediment|sediment]], and a smaller number float as [[Plankton|plankton]]. Their shells, or tests, are commonly made of [[Calcium carbonate|calcium carbonate]] or agglutinated sediment particles. More than 50,000 species are recognized, both living (6,700–10,000) and [[Fossil|fossil]] (40,000). Most are under 1 mm, although the largest reach 20 cm. Fossil forams allow precise correlation of sedimentary layers, and planktonic species serve as proxies for past ocean temperatures. Benthic assemblages help assess seafloor pollution and locate [[Petroleum|petroleum]] deposits.

American business magazine founded in 1917 by B. C. Forbes. Published eight times a year, it covers [[Finance|finance]], industry, investing and [[Marketing|marketing]], and also reports on [[Technology|technology]], science, politics and law. It is known for lists such as the Forbes 400 of the richest Americans and the Forbes Global 2000 of the world's top companies. Since 2014 it has been owned by the [[Hong Kong]]-based investment group Integrated Whale Media Investments. It is headquartered in Jersey City, New Jersey.

Imperial palace complex in the center of [[Beijing]], China. It was the residence of 24 [[Ming dynasty|Ming]] and [[Qing dynasty|Qing]] emperors and the center of Chinese political power from 1420 to 1924. Built from 1406 to 1420 under the [[Yongle Emperor]], after the capital moved from [[Nanjing]] to Beijing, it covers about 72 hectares (180 acres). Its name reflects its enormous scale and the severely restricted access to all but the emperor, the imperial family and their eunuch servants, and unauthorized entry was punishable by death. The Chinese name Zijincheng, meaning Purple Forbidden City, first formally appeared in 1576. It has been a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site since 1987, and since 2012 it has averaged 14 million visitors a year.

American car produced by the [[Ford Motor Company]] from 1908 to 1927. Generally regarded as the first mass-affordable automobile, it was built on [[Assembly line|assembly lines]] with [[Interchangeable parts|interchangeable parts]], and its price fell from $780 in 1910 to $290 in 1924. Designed mainly by Joseph A. Galamb, Eugene Farkas and Childe Harold Wills, it was nicknamed the Tin Lizzie. With over 15 million sold, it was the best-selling car in history until the [[Volkswagen Beetle]] overtook it in 1972. It symbolized innovation for the rising American middle class.

American multinational automobile manufacturer headquartered in Dearborn, [[Michigan]]. Founded by [[Henry Ford]] and incorporated on June 16, 1903, it sells cars and commercial vehicles under the Ford brand, and luxury cars under Lincoln. It pioneered large-scale manufacturing with [[Assembly line|moving assembly lines]], methods known around the world by 1914 as Fordism. It is listed on the [[New York Stock Exchange]] under the ticker F, but the Ford family retains 40 percent of the voting rights through special Class B shares. It is the second-largest American-based automaker, behind [[General Motors]]. In 2023 it produced 4.4 million automobiles and employed about 177,000 people. During the 2008–2010 industry crisis it did not require a federal government rescue, unlike two other major US automakers.

American [[Car|car]] manufactured and marketed by [[Ford Motor Company|Ford]] since 1964, and the namesake of the pony car segment. Introduced on April 17, 1964, it sold over 400,000 units in its first year. Its success led to competitors including the Chevrolet Camaro and Dodge Challenger. It is Ford's longest nameplate in continuous production, and its seventh generation is the fifth-best-selling Ford car nameplate.

Application of science to law, generally criminal and civil, also known as criminalistics. Forensic scientists collect, preserve and analyze evidence such as DNA, fingerprints, bloodstain patterns, firearms, [[Ballistics|ballistics]], [[Toxicology|toxicology]] and fire debris. Some work at crime scenes, others in laboratories, and others on financial data, and they testify as expert witnesses for either prosecution or defense. The first written account of using medicine and [[Insect|entomology]] to solve crimes is the book *Xi Yuan Lu* (translated as *Washing Away of Wrongs*), written in China in 1248 by Song Ci during the [[Song dynasty]]. It introduced regulations on [[Autopsy|autopsy]] reports to court and distinguished suicide from faked suicide. In the 1890s Francis Galton validated [[Fingerprint|fingerprints]] as unique identifiers.

Set of emotionally and physically intimate acts meant to create sexual arousal and desire for sexual activity. It can include [[Kiss|kissing]], sexual touching, removing clothes, [[Oral sex|oral sex]], manual sex, sexual games and roleplay, and in some contexts nonphysical acts. Physically, the sexual organs of both partners receive more blood flow and become sensitive; in female partners this produces clitoral erection and vaginal lubrication, and a lack of lubrication may cause dyspareunia. Psychologically, foreplay lowers inhibitions and increases emotional intimacy. Foreplay has been found to be positively associated with female [[Orgasm|orgasm]]. In a survey of 152 mainly university-educated heterosexual couples, neither partner was satisfied with the duration of foreplay; the average was 12 minutes of foreplay and 7 minutes of intercourse.

Double-layered fold of skin and mucosal tissue covering the [[Glans penis|glans]] of the [[Human penis|penis]]. Also called the prepuce, it is attached to the glans by the frenulum and keeps the glans moist. It is generally fused to the glans at birth and separates before or during [[Puberty]], after which it is typically retractable. The male prepuce is homologous to the clitoral hood in females. Proponents of [[Circumcision|circumcision]], which removes the foreskin, cite reduced risks of urinary tract infections and penile cancer, while critics argue that non-therapeutic infant circumcision infringes bodily autonomy.

Science and craft of creating, managing, planting, using, conserving and repairing [[Forest|forests]] and woodlands for human and environmental benefit. Modern forestry pursues multiple-use management, including timber, fuelwood, wildlife [[Habitat|habitat]], water quality, recreation, biodiversity, erosion control and preserving forests as sinks for [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Silviculture is the commercial practice of forest management, primarily for timber production. In Germany, forests cover nearly a third of the land area, and forestry supports more than a million jobs and about €181 billion of value a year. Worldwide, an estimated 880 million people spend part of their time collecting firewood or producing [[Charcoal|charcoal]], many of them women. Genetic diversity in planting stock is needed to maintain forest vitality and resilience to pests and [[Disease|diseases]].

Manufacturing process that shapes [[Metal|metal]] using localized compressive forces from a [[Hammer|hammer]] or die. Forging is classified by temperature as cold, warm or hot. Hot forging, above the metal's recrystallization temperature, can be done more quickly and precisely, while cold forging typically causes work hardening. Forged parts range in weight from less than a kilogram to hundreds of metric tons. Smiths have made kitchenware, hand tools, edged weapons, [[Cymbal|cymbals]] and [[Jewellery|jewelry]] for millennia. Since the [[Industrial Revolution]], forged components have been used wherever high strength is required, and forging is now a major worldwide industry.

Renunciation or cessation of resentment, indignation or [[Anger|anger]] toward someone who has caused harm. Psychologically, forgiveness is distinct from condoning, excusing or forgetting, and theorists differ on whether it requires reconciliation with the offender. Most world [[Religion|religions]] teach forgiveness, including [[Judaism]], [[Islam]] and [[Jainism]]. Robert Enright of the University of Wisconsin–Madison developed a 20-step process model. Studies associate forgiveness with better health: people who think about forgiving an offender show improved cardiovascular and nervous system functioning, and more forgiving people report fewer illnesses. Fred Luskin of [[Stanford University]] presented evidence that forgiveness can be learned.

Eating utensil with a long handle ending in a head that branches into several narrow tines for spearing food. Bone forks have been found at sites of the [[Bronze Age]] Qijia culture (2400–1900 BC) and in the [[Shang dynasty]] (c. 1600–c. 1050 BC). Forks were used as cooking and serving utensils in ancient Egypt and the [[Roman Empire]], while the personal table fork was most likely invented in the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, where it was in common use by the 4th century. By the 11th century it had spread through Italy, where it displaced the long wooden spike used for [[Pasta|pasta]]. It was introduced to the French court with the entourage of [[Catherine de' Medici]]. Its use spread more slowly in northern Europe, and it became common in Great Britain only in the 18th century.
